verdicts.argument: The mutant seeds the accumulator with one extra segment whose value is the constant string `Stryker was here`. Two facts make it unable to move anything. First, `splitSegments` has exactly one consumer in the tree — the `for (const segment of splitSegments(evidence))` loop in `parseEvidencePointers` (grep over src/ and dist/ returns that call site and nothing else) — and the only way a segment becomes anything at all is `chunk.trim().match(POINTER_PREFIX)` with `POINTER_PREFIX = /\b(file|test|adr):(\S.*)$/`. That pattern requires the literal text `file:`, `test:` or `adr:`; the injected string contains no `:` character at all, so no chunk derived from it can ever produce a pointer, and a segment that produces no pointer contributes nothing to the returned array. Second, the element is PREPENDED to the array, so every segment cut from the operator's own cell is byte-identical to the pristine one. The function's output therefore differs by one inert element, and the array of pointers — the only thing any caller ever sees — cannot differ for ANY cell. No mission can distinguish it, because a mission can only ever supply a cell, and the cell's parse is unchanged.

Parse-level: 0 differing pointer arrays over 1 410 designed cells (including `file:code/b.ts#"the exact ; sentence"`, `;file:code/b.ts;`, unclosed quotes and every whitespace/terminator in every position) and 0 over 40 000 fuzzed cells.
verdicts.argument: The mutant makes the FIRST segment carry the prefix `Stryker was here!`. Three separate reasons close every path by which that could move a pointer. (1) It cannot CREATE one: the literal has no `:`, and `POINTER_PREFIX` needs `file:`, `test:` or `adr:`. (2) It cannot DESTROY one: the pattern is unanchored at the front, so text before the pointer is simply skipped, and its `\b` is satisfied whatever follows the prefix, because the prefix's last character is `!`, a non-word character, so the transition to the `f` of `file:` is always a word boundary. (3) It cannot MOVE a cut: the segment is handed to `splitPointers`, whose decision at each index is `/(^|[\s,])(file|test|adr):\S/.test(segment.slice(i))`. Prepending a constant shifts every index of the operator's text by the same constant length, and `segment.slice(i)` at the shifted index is the very same suffix — so every cut taken inside the operator's text is taken identically. The only new behaviour is cuts INSIDE the prefix (at its two spaces), which can only yield extra chunks made of `Stryker` and `was`, again `:`-free and therefore pointer-free; whatever remains of the prefix stays glued in front of the operator's text as `here!`, which is the boundary case already covered by (2). Finally the prefix cannot change `chunk.trim()` in any way that matters: a chunk that used to trim to `""` now trims to `Stryker was here!`, and neither string matches `POINTER_PREFIX`.

verdicts.argument: Same mechanism as the line-38 mutant, applied to every segment AFTER the first: instead of restarting the buffer empty after a `;`, it restarts it with `Stryker was here!`. The three closures are identical and each is independent of which segment is concerned. (1) No `:` in the literal, so no chunk it appears in can match `POINTER_PREFIX = /\b(file|test|adr):(\S.*)$/`, hence no pointer is created. (2) The pattern is unanchored at the front and the literal ends in `!`, a non-word character, so the `\b` before `file:`/`test:`/`adr:` still holds and no existing pointer is destroyed. (3) The prefix lives at the head of the segment, and `splitPointers` decides each cut from `segment.slice(i)`, a suffix that the prefix leaves untouched — so no cut inside the operator's text moves; cuts inside the prefix itself yield only `:`-free chunks. Note the quote state is untouched by the mutant: a `;` inside a quoted symbol never reaches this branch at all, which is why the green row `file:code/b.ts#"the exact ; sentence"` in m1 stays green under the mutant exactly as in baseline.
